Key Points 
Interested in onsemi? Here are five stocks we like better. 
AI data-center growth is a central focus: onsemi expects AI data-center revenue to exceed $500 million in 2026, potentially surpass $2.5 billion by 2030, as higher-voltage infrastructure increases its semiconductor content opportunity per rack. 
The company introduced its Embedded Power Platform and highlighted vertical gallium nitride and silicon carbide technologies to improve power density, efficiency and thermal performance across AI, automotive and industrial applications. 
onsemi set ambitious 2030 financial targets: 12%–14% annual revenue growth, nearly $11 billion in revenue, 53% gross margins, 38% operating margins and more than $3.5 billion in free cash flow, while planning to return 100% of free cash flow to shareholders after investments and acquisitions. 
3 Robotics Stocks Under $10: Value, Momentum, or Bet? 
onsemi (NASDAQ:ON) outlined a strategy centered on power-density technologies for artificial intelligence data centers, electric vehicles, industrial systems and "Physical AI," while setting long-term revenue, margin and free-cash-flow targets through 2030. 
At the company's analyst event, President and CEO Hassane El-Khoury said AI infrastructure is increasingly constrained not only by compute and memory, but by the ability to efficiently deliver and manage power. He said future systems will require power that is distributed, efficient and able to operate under sustained peak loads. 
→ IonQ and NVIDIA Just Cracked a Major Quantum Computing Bottleneck 
MarketBeat Week in Review – 08/03 - 08/07 
"More power is really not enough," El-Khoury said. "We need better power." 
Embedded Power Platform and high-voltage technologies 
The company introduced its Embedded Power Platform, or EPP, which it described as a platform rather than a single product. EPP uses a silicon wafer as an active package and embeds heterogeneous semiconductor products, including silicon carbide and gallium nitride components, into a wafer-level architecture. onsemi said the approach is intended to improve electrical, thermal and mechanical performance simultaneously while reducing system-development time. 
→ 2 Stocks Breaking Out Post-FOMC With One Thing in Common 
The AI Chip Stock Making a Quiet Move Toward Dominance 
El-Khoury said EPP is already being sampled for automotive, industrial and AI data-center applications using the company's existing 12-inch manufacturing process. He said the platform can be used with onsemi's high-voltage technologies and its Treo intelligence platform, which is designed to support modular power-control solutions across voltage levels and end markets. 
Story Continues 
The company also highlighted vertical gallium nitride, or vGaN, technology. El-Khoury said onsemi has developed, sampled and manufactured vertical GaN devices that have been placed on customer boards for automotive, industrial and AI data-center applications. He said production is supported by the company's Syracuse facility and would not require a new greenfield fab investment. 
→ Generac Plugs into Amazon for an $8B AI-Powered Deal 
Subaru said it is evaluating onsemi's embedded power module technology for future vehicle platforms. A Subaru representative said the technology could offer higher power density, dual-sided cooling, improved electrical control and system-level cost reductions, though the automaker said it continues to evaluate how the technology may fit into its vehicle plans. 
AI data-center opportunity 
Achyut Shah, president of onsemi's Power Solutions Group, said AI processors are moving from consuming hundreds of watts toward kilowatt-scale power requirements, while rack-level power needs are rising from tens of kilowatts toward megawatts. He said this transition will require a shift from traditional AC distribution architectures to high-voltage DC systems extending from the grid to computing equipment. 
Shah said the initial transition toward higher-voltage rack designs and sidecar architectures is expected to begin ramping in the next 12 to 18 months. He said broader adoption of solid-state transformers could begin around late 2028 or early 2029. 
According to Shah, onsemi estimates its semiconductor content opportunity could increase from about $15,000 per rack to more than $115,000 per rack as data-center infrastructure transitions to higher-voltage architectures. He said the company expects AI data-center revenue to exceed $500 million in 2026, more than double from the prior year, and to double again in 2027. The company's long-term model assumes AI data-center revenue grows at least 10 percentage points faster than the underlying market through 2030. 
Using a hypothetical 40% market compound annual growth rate, Shah said onsemi projects its AI data-center revenue could grow at least 50% annually from a $500 million base in 2026 to more than $2.5 billion in 2030. 
The company cited several claimed product-performance benchmarks, including an 800-volt-to-6-volt or 12-volt conversion system using vGaN that it said offers 20% better efficiency and 20% lower size than competing solutions. It also described an EPP-based silicon carbide JFET solid-state circuit-breaker design that it said is 50% smaller and operates 20% cooler than the nearest competing product. 
Shah also announced that onsemi won a "major" Vcore socket, with revenue expected to begin by the end of 2026. 
Automotive and industrial growth plans 
Sudhir Gopalswamy, group president for Intelligent Sensing and Analog and Mixed-Signal Group, said onsemi expects automotive revenue to grow about 9% annually from 2026 through 2030, despite the company's assumption that global light-vehicle production, or SAAR, remains flat during that period. 
The automotive strategy is built around electrification, autonomous-driving content and software-defined vehicles using zonal electrical architectures. Gopalswamy said the company plans to continue advancing silicon carbide performance, increase device-voltage capability toward 1,400 volts to support 1,000-volt batteries, and introduce intelligent current controllers for traction inverters. 
He said onsemi is sampling an intelligent silicon carbide current-controller solution this month. The company expects the pairing of current sensing and control capabilities to provide a "one-generation" performance improvement while reducing certain system bill-of-materials costs. 
For EPP-based traction inverters, Gopalswamy said the platform could double power while using half the area, resulting in four times the power density. He also projected that onsemi's opportunity across electrification, advanced driver-assistance systems and zonal architectures could reach up to $2,000 of content per vehicle. 
In industrial markets, the company is targeting 10% growth through 2030, supported by grid upgrades, energy infrastructure, industrial automation and the broader AI-driven demand for power systems. Gopalswamy said Physical AI applications, excluding automotive, represent a potential $6 billion addressable market for onsemi by 2030. He said humanoid robots could represent about $900 of potential company content per unit by that year. 
Financial targets and capital allocation 
CFO Thad Trent said onsemi has invested $8.7 billion over the past five years, including $3.6 billion in research and development, $800 million for five tuck-in acquisitions and $4.3 billion in capital expenditures. He said the investments were directed toward power platforms, sensing, silicon carbide, vertical GaN and manufacturing capacity. 
Trent said the company expects its addressable market to expand by $81 billion, including $45 billion related to AI data centers, $20 billion in automotive and $16 billion in industrial markets. 
Company revenue growth target of 12% to 14% annually from 2026 through 2030. 
Revenue of just under $11 billion in 2030, based on 2026 Street consensus as the baseline. 
Gross-margin target of 53%. 
Operating-margin target of 38%. 
Capital intensity of about 5% of revenue. 
Free-cash-flow margin target of 30% to 35%, with free cash flow exceeding $3.5 billion in 2030. 
Trent said the financial model excludes the proposed Synaptics transaction. He said onsemi expects Synaptics, if the deal closes, to grow at more than 15% over the long term, generate gross margins above 55% and produce more than $200 million in synergies over the first 18 months. 
The company said it plans to continue investing in organic growth and acquisitions, maintain balance-sheet flexibility and return 100% of free cash flow to shareholders after those priorities. Trent said onsemi has $5.3 billion remaining under its existing share-repurchase authorization. 
About onsemi (NASDAQ:ON) 
onsemi is engaged in disruptive innovations and also a supplier of power and analog semiconductors. The firm offers vehicle electrification and safety, sustainable energy grids, industrial automation, and 5G and cloud infrastructure, with a focus on automotive and industrial end-markets. It operates through the following segments: Power Solutions Group, Advanced Solutions Group, and Intelligent Sensing Group. The Power Solutions Group segment offers discrete, module, and semiconductor products that perform multiple application functions, including power switching, power conversion, signal conditioning, circuit protection, signal amplification, and voltage reference functions.

content_text:
TOPPAN Group Inaugurates New BOPP Film Manufacturing Line at Irplast in Italy
Enhancing supply capabilities using simultaneous biaxial orientation technology to bolster global supply of sustainable solutions
Tweet 
Tokyo – September 17, 2026 – TOPPAN Inc. (TOPPAN), a TOPPAN Group company and wholly owned subsidiary of TOPPAN Holdings Inc. (TYO: 7911), and its Italy-based film manufacturing subsidiary Irplast S.p.A. (Irplast), today announced the inauguration of a new manufacturing line for high-performance biaxially oriented polypropylene (BOPP) films, marking the occasion with a ceremony on September 15, 2026.
An overview of this development will be included at the TOPPAN booth (East Hall 2, Booth No. 2R10) during TOKYO PACK 2026, to be held at Tokyo Big Sight from Wednesday, October 14 to Friday, October 16, 2026.
Background and Objectives
In its packaging business, the TOPPAN Group is accelerating the establishment of its global supply network for recycle-ready mono-material packaging to meet tightening environmental regulations - such as the EU Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (PPWR) - and to drive the transition toward a circular economy.
Irplast, a TOPPAN Group company, is a premium film manufacturer equipped with advanced simultaneous biaxial orientation technology. Its unique expertise in minimizing thermal shrinkage provides BOPP films with exceptional heat resistance, mechanical strength, and superior transparency.
Through the operation of this line, together with existing capabilities, the plant will be able to establish an overall supply infrastructure of up to 30,000 tonnes per year for high-performance BOPP films. This deployment expands the TOPPAN Group’s production capabilities and enhances manufacturing efficiency, ensuring a stable, local supply to meet the surging demand for sustainable packaging in Europe and beyond.
Features of the New Manufacturing Line
・Developing High-Value Applications through Simultaneous Orientation Technology: 
The films produced on this line offer uniform physical properties and high dimensional stability achieved through the LISIM 1 simultaneous stretching process. Leveraging this robustness, TOPPAN and Irplast will actively develop high-end packaging applications that require durability even under demanding conditions, such as retort sterilization.
・Reducing Environmental Impact through Package Down Gauging: 
Utilizing the film’s superior mechanical strength, development will be focused toward "down gauging" (reducing film thickness). This enables a steady and continuous reduction in plastic consumption while maintaining essential packaging functions, directly supporting resource conservation goals.
Future Activities
The new line is expected to commence full commercial operations by late 2026, supplying high-performance BOPP films to packaging converters and global brand owners.
The combination of Irplast’s BOPP film manufacturing expertise and the TOPPAN Group’s broad base of technologies and solutions will expand sustainable solutions worldwide by driving use as a next-generation substrate in transparent GL BARRIER 2 films as well as unlocking new possibilities for high-performance, sustainable packaging solutions that contribute to a circular economy.
1 LISIM is Bruckner’s simultaneous stretching technology utilized by Irplast.
URL: https://www.irplast.com/bopp-film-division/ 
2 GL BARRIER is TOPPAN’s proprietary brand of transparent film products that deliver world-class barrier performance. Stable performance is enabled by a multi-layer structure combining a unique coating layer with a high-quality vapor-deposited layer. In recognition of their numerous outstanding features, GL BARRIER products are used in a wide variety of fields, including the food, healthcare/pharmaceutical, and industrial materials sectors. Combining the functions of the printing and barrier substrate layers into a single layer provides an alternative to aluminum foil with a streamlined layer structure.
https://www.toppan.com/en/living-industry/packaging/products/barrier_film/ 
About the TOPPAN Group
Established in Tokyo in 1900, the TOPPAN Group is a leading and diversified global provider committed to delivering sustainable, integrated solutions in fields including printing, communications, security, packaging, décor materials, electronics, and digital transformation. The TOPPAN Group’s global team of more than 50,000 employees offers optimal solutions enabled by industry-leading expertise and technologies to address the diverse challenges of every business sector and society and contribute to the achievement of shared sustainability goals.

Hexagon refocuses on automation options
The report provides gradual automation choices from turnkey inspection cells to customized production workflows
Sept. 16, 2026
3 min read 
Add Us On Google 
An engineer programs or repairs a high-tech industrial robot. This smart factory uses AI-driven automation for advanced manufacturing or microchip production. 
Hexagon reported Sept. 14 that manufacturers know automation is essential for staying competitive. However, according to its upcoming “Americas state of manufacturing survey,” when it comes to automation, only 24% believe they are ahead of competitors, 46% are keeping pace, 30% are behind or have not started. Meanwhile, 85% report at least one barrier to accelerating AI and automation.
For years, manufacturers often had to choose between buying an off-the-shelf automation system that might not fit their production requirements or investing in a custom automation project that required added engineering resources, systems integration and upfront investment. As a result, Hexagon reports many automation initiatives stall before they begin.
Consequently, Hexagon’s portable metrology division has refocused on more practical, achievable, gradual automation. Rather than asking users to leap into automation all at once, it’s giving them options for expanding automation as their production requirements increase. This is expected to help users automate at a pace that aligns with their production needs with pathways ranging from ready-to-deploy inspection cells to fully customized automation solutions built with integration partners.
"Automation shouldn't require manufacturers to choose between a rigid, one-size-fits-all system and an overwhelming custom engineering project,” says Joel Martin, product management director in Hexagon Manufacturing Intelligence’s portable division. "Our goal is to give manufacturers practical options that let them automate today, while leaving room to grow tomorrow."
To lower the barriers to adopting automation, beyond simply reducing costs, Hexagon adds it’s making automation easier to deploy, operate and integrate into day-to-day production, particularly for manufacturers that may not have dedicated automation expertise. This means creating more entry points into automation, while giving users the flexibility to scale as their needs evolve.
For example, Hexagon’s Presto standardized, robotic inspection cells, combine industrial robotics, metrology technology and automation software to bring automated quality inspection closer to production. More specifically, Hexagon is previewing its Presto XS entry point to automated metrology within Presto’s Quality Stations ecosystem at this week’s International Manufacturing Technology Show in Chicago.
Designed for small, complex parts, Presto XS brings industrial metrology into a compact, mobile system that can move closer to production, and operate in space-constrained environments with minimal infrastructure changes. Its intuitive, plant-floor interface lets user create and edit inspection routines without robot programming expertise, enabling users to implement automated inspection without typical automation complexities.
Presto XS also supports flexible, two-in-one workflows, which let manufacturers use it as an automated cobot or handheld scanner as inspection demands change. This flexibility lets users reduce inspection cycle times and transport delays, free skilled metrology experts from repetitive scanning tasks, and standardize quality processes across multiple stations.
Hexagon adds its IMTS exhibit will also demonstrate how automation doesn't have to begin with a robot. Manufacturers can start by using portable metrology systems, including handheld scanners, laser trackers and optical measurement technologies for manual inspection. As production volumes increase, those measurement technologies can be integrated into robotic inspection cells or automated workflows without requiring users to replace sensors they already invested in. This approach reduces retraining, preserves existing measurement workflows, and provides a practical path from manual inspection to automation at each user’s own pace.
The exhibit will also feature Hexagon's Leica Absolute Tracker ATS800 two-in-one laser tracker integrated on an autonomous mobile robot (AMR), which will show how optical measurement technology can support customized automation workflows for large-scale manufacturing applications. Designed for industries such as aerospace and shipbuilding, where moving large parts to a fixed inspection station is often impractical, ATS800 illustrates how manufacturers can bring inspection directly into production, enabling quality data to guide manufacturing decisions earlier in the process, rather than waiting until after production.

Asahi Kasei Launches VANTIJ SU-VFC Benchtop
New platform streamlines small-scale virus filtration for biopharma and gene therapy workflows. 
September 15, 2026 
By: Charlie Sternberg 
Associate Editor , Contract Pharma 
Save 
The VANTIJ SU-VFC Benchtop. 
Asahi Kasei Bioprocess , a subsidiary of diversified global company Asahi Kasei , has introduced the VANTIJ SU-VFC Benchtop, expanding its VANTIJ family with the line’s first benchtop-scale platform.
The compact system is designed to streamline small-scale virus filtration by bringing the automation, repeatability, and operator-focused design principles of the broader VANTIJ portfolio to benchtop workflows. It supports 0.12 m² or 0.3 m² Planova 35N virus-removal filters and provides the process control and data-focused capabilities needed for modern biopharmaceutical development.
Initially designed for gene therapy manufacturing, the VANTIJ SU-VFC Benchtop addresses common development challenges such as long production timelines, complex regulatory requirements, operator training demands, and therapy-specific process needs. The platform is built to reduce those burdens through a guided shadow-board layout, tool-free tube set installation and replacement, intuitive connection points, and recipe-driven software. It also enables batch reporting and supports consistent execution of critical filtration processes.
“The biopharmaceutical industry continues to pursue more efficient pathways for bringing innovative therapies to patients,” said Chris Rombach, President of Asahi Kasei Bioprocess America. “The VANTIJ SU-VFC Benchtop reflects Asahi Kasei Bioprocess’s commitment to supporting manufacturers with solutions that simplify critical process steps while delivering the confidence and reliability associated with Planova virus filtration and the Asahi Kasei name.”
The launch highlights Asahi Kasei’s broader push to support the growth of cell and gene therapies, among the biopharmaceutical industry’s fastest-evolving segments. As a strategic focus within the company’s Healthcare sector, these emerging modalities remain central to Asahi Kasei’s Life Science growth strategy.

From electronics to agriculture: How 3M film technology is helping manage light in new ways
Sep 15, 2026
Print current page. 
Send current page by email. 
Share current page on facebook. 
Share on Linkedin. 
Share current page on X 
For decades, 3M has applied optical film technology to help manage light in precise and useful ways, including in electronic devices and displays where light control can support brightness, clarity and energy efficiency. Now, that same expertise is being adapted for a new challenge: filtering sunlight to help support agriculture while also helping generate renewable energy.
Through an ongoing partnership with Voltiris , 3M is helping advance spectral-filtering solar technology designed to selectively manage sunlight above crops. The approach aims to let plants receive the light they need for growth while redirecting other portions of the light spectrum they don’t to help generate electricity.
Building on work in greenhouse agriculture, the companies recently launched an outdoor pilot in the Canary Islands to test how Voltiris’ Voltimax spectral-filtering module performs in open-field conditions.
For 3M, the pilot is part of a bigger story: applying an existing technology platform in a new way through external collaboration.
Your browser does not support the video tag. 
A new use for a core 3M technology platform 
3M’s role in the Voltiris partnership is rooted in its long-standing expertise in optical films, materials science and light management.
Optical films are designed to control how light is transmitted, reflected or redirected. In this pilot application, that expertise helps support a system that filters sunlight above crops, balancing two goals that are often in tension: protecting plants from excess heat while capturing solar energy.
That capability is what makes the collaboration different from a traditional solar installation. Rather than simply placing panels near agricultural land, the technology is designed to work with the growing environment by managing the spectrum of light reaching the crops.
For growers, that could create a valuable combination: improved growing conditions and renewable energy generation from the same footprint.
Why the Canary Islands pilot matters now 
The new pilot is in Gran Canaria, Spain, over a banana farm operated by Grupo FSM, the largest banana producer and exporter in Europe.
Bananas are central to the region’s agricultural economy, but they are grown in a challenging environment with high solar irradiance and significant heat stress. A large share of irrigation relies on desalinated water, where production requires substantial amounts of energy. In the Canary Islands, the electricity used for desalination represents a significant share of the total cost of banana production.
That makes the region a strong test case for a solution designed to address multiple pressures at once.
The pilot will explore whether spectral-filtering solar technology can help reduce heat stress for crops while also generating electricity that is expected to partially supply a desalination plant used for irrigation.
From greenhouse innovation to open-field agriculture 
3M and Voltiris have been working together for several years to help move the technology from concept toward broader application.
The solution has already been deployed at industrial scale in greenhouses across Europe. The Canary Islands pilot represents the next step: testing how the technology performs outdoors, where conditions are less controlled and durability, system performance and environmental exposure become even more important.
That shift from greenhouse to open-field agriculture is a meaningful expansion of the opportunity.
It also reflects how 3M works with partners to advance innovation: combining 3M’s science, technology platforms and application expertise with external companies developing new market solutions.
“In high-tech greenhouses across Northern Europe, where every percentage point of light matters, our technology has demonstrated that crops can thrive beneath Voltiris modules. Results show plant temperatures reduced by around 4°C and irrigation needs lowered by approximately 20%,” said Jonas Roch, chief technology officer and co-founder of Voltiris. “As heatwaves become more frequent and intense, our agrivoltaic solution helps make agriculture more resilient. We are now bringing the same principle outdoors, with the potential to deliver similar - or even greater - benefits while also protecting crops from wind, frost, hail, and heavy rain.”
Innovation through partnership 
“The collaboration with Voltiris demonstrates the value of combining 3M’s materials science expertise with external innovation to help accelerate emerging technologies,” said Mark Copman, senior vice president of 3M Ventures. “Together, we are advancing solutions that have the potential to support both agriculture and energy, while reflecting 3M’s ongoing commitment to applying science to complex global challenges.”
The partnership is an example of the way 3M works with innovators across industries: taking core technology platforms and applying them in new ways to help solve customer and market challenges.
In this case, 3M’s optical film expertise is helping enable a new approach to agricultural solar technology - one that could support crop environments, help generate renewable power and address resource pressures in regions where sunlight is abundant but conditions are increasingly demanding.
FAQ 
What is 3M’s partnership with Voltiris? 
3M is working with Voltiris to help advance spectral-filtering solar technology for agriculture. The collaboration combines Voltiris’ solar module innovation with 3M’s materials science and optical film expertise to explore new ways of managing sunlight above crops.
What role does 3M technology play? 
3M contributes expertise in optical films and light management. In this application, that technology helps support a system designed to filter sunlight so crops can receive the light they need while other portions of the spectrum are redirected to generate electricity.
What is new about the Canary Islands pilot? 
The Canary Islands pilot is the first outdoor deployment of Voltiris’ Voltimax spectral-filtering solar module for open-field agriculture. It provides a real-world test in a region where banana growers face high solar exposure, crop heat stress and energy-intensive irrigation needs.
How does this reflect 3M innovation? 
The partnership shows how 3M can apply a core technology platform in a new way through collaboration. By adapting optical film expertise for agriculture and renewable energy, 3M is helping advance a solution designed to address multiple challenges at once: crop conditions, energy generation and resource efficiency.

New optical tracking system combines fully wireless operation, dynamic tracking and portability to simplify shop floor and field-based inspection

A 3D scanner. The Hyperscan SR is designed to simplify high-accuracy 3D scanning on the shop floor and in the field.
(Provided by Dragonite_East/iStock Photo) 
Hexagon’s Manufacturing Intelligence Business Area previewed HYPERSCAN SR, a fully wireless optical tracking 3D scanner and the new entry point to its HYPERSCAN series , shown for the first time at IMTS 2026 (Booth #134102).
Manufacturers increasingly need to inspect parts where the work happens, whether that's on the production line, across multiple facilities or out in the field. While optical tracking makes it possible to capture accurate measurements even when parts or their surroundings are moving, traditional systems often require cables, time-consuming setup and specialized operators. HYPERSCAN SR removes those barriers, making high-accuracy optical tracking more practical for everyday manufacturing. 
Natively fully wireless, with WiFi 6 connectivity and battery power, HYPERSCAN SR deploys quickly and is straightforward for non-specialist operators to run. Its dynamic tracking follows both the part and the scanner at once, so movement and vibration do not interrupt the scan.
A wide scanning area, multiple scanning modes with hole flash capture and edge detection, and target-free scanning make it productive across a broad range of parts, and it is ready for integration onto a cobot or industrial robot.
HYPERSCAN SR joins HYPERSCAN Ultra and HYPERSCAN Super to complete Hexagon's optical scanning portfolio . HYPERSCAN SR offers a fully wireless, highly portable entry point, HYPERSCAN Ultra is designed for everyday production scanning, and HYPERSCAN Super delivers maximum range and performance for large-scale parts and automated inspection.
All three systems share the same workflows and coordinate system, making it easy to scale as measurement needs evolve. 
"Dynamic optical tracking keeps a scan stable even when the part moves or the setup vibrates, because the scanner and the part are tracked together in one coordinate system," said Darren Goh, Product Director, Handheld 3D Scanners, Hexagon’s Portable Metrology division. "HYPERSCAN SR builds that into a fully wireless system, with WiFi 6 and battery power native to the device rather than added on. It's quick to deploy and simple enough for everyday operators to run, so teams can bring it into limited-access and power-limited areas that a larger, cabled setup can't reach." 
HYPERSCAN SR is designed for applications where mobility matters most, including on-site and in-field inspection, supplier and incoming-goods verification, field service and maintenance, tooling and fixture inspection, and decentralized quality control. It is well suited for manufacturers across automotive, rail, energy, construction, industrial equipment, consumer products and general manufacturing. 
"North American manufacturers are inspecting more parts on the shop floor and in the field than ever before, and they want technology their own teams can deploy with confidence,” said Joel Martin, Director of Product Management, Portable Division, at Hexagon Manufacturing Intelligence.
“HYPERSCAN SR meets that need with a fully wireless design that's quick to set up, easy to operate and provides a straightforward path into optical tracking without the complexity of traditional systems.”
HYPERSCAN SR is on display at IMTS 2026 at McCormick Place, Chicago, from 14 to 19 September at Booth #13410. The product will be officially launched, with availability and pricing details later this year – register here to find out more.

content_text:
HS Hyosung Energy Solution Korea a joint venture between HS Hyosung Group and Belgian materials company Umicore, will invest 1.2 trillion won to build a silicon anode materials production base in Ulsan.
​HS Hyosung Energy Solution Korea said Sept. 14 that it signed a memorandum of understanding with Ulsan Metropolitan City to build a silicon anode materials production plant. The company plans to invest a total of 1.2 trillion won through 2030 at the Ulsan-Mipo National Industrial Complex.
​The investment will be carried out in three phases. In the first phase, the company will invest 300 billion won to build MPK-1, a silicon anode materials plant with an annual capacity of 5,000 tons, by the first quarter of 2028. Further investment will follow to establish a mass-production system.
​Silicon anode materials have a higher energy density than conventional graphite-based anode materials, allowing electric vehicles to travel farther and charge faster.
​HS Hyosung Energy Solution Korea was established by HS Hyosung Group and Umicore for the silicon anode materials business, with an 80% to 20% ownership split. The venture is the first new business pursued by HS Hyosung Group since its separation from the wider Hyosung Group.
​Lee Ki-soo, chief executive officer of HS Hyosung Energy Solution Korea, said, "As we have selected Ulsan as our first investment site, we will grow together with the region by building an advanced production base and creating jobs."

EPC releases two new white papers on GaN power conversion
Monday 14th September 2026
Technical papers examine 800 VDC power delivery for AI infrastructure and integrated 100 V GaN power stages for robotics, drones, and motion control 
Efficient Power Conversion (EPC) has published two new technical white papers addressing critical power-conversion challenges in two rapidly evolving markets: AI data centres and high-performance multi-axis motor drives.
The first white paper, 'GaN-Based Power Delivery in AI data centres: High-Density Power Conversion Architectures from 800 VDC to Point-of-Load' examines the transition toward 800 VDC distribution as AI racks move from tens of kilowatts toward hundreds of kilowatts and megawatt-scale compute clusters. At 800 VDC, a 200 kW rack requires only one-sixteenth of the current of a 48 V distribution bus, reducing conductor size, I²R losses, and cooling requirements. 
The paper explores three architectures for converting 800 VDC to 50 V, 12.5 V, and 6.25 V rails, with particular focus on modular Input-Series, Output-Parallel (ISOP) LLC converters. By dividing the high-voltage input among multiple modules, the architecture enables low-voltage GaN FETs with a better Figure of Merit, when compared to higher-voltage devices, to perform high-ratio conversion at high switching frequencies. 
Practical results demonstrate the performance potential: an 800 V-to-50 V implementation reaches 98.6 percent peak efficiency, while the EPC91123 800 V-to-12.5 V converter achieves 98.2 percent peak efficiency in an 8 mm profile. A 6 kW 800 V-to-6.25 V architecture reaches 98 percent peak and 97 percent full-load efficiency. 
“As GPU power continues to increase, power conversion must move closer to the processor while minimising conversion stages,” said Jason Zhang, Vice President of DC-DC Marketing and System Engineering at EPC. “Gen 7 GaN combined with modular ISOP architectures provides a practical path from an 800 VDC backbone to the very low bus voltages and extremely high currents required by next-generation AI processors.”
The second white paper, 'From Device to Platform: EPC23108/09/10/11 100 V Integrated GaN Power Stages Simplify Multi-Axis Motor Drive Design', addresses the increasing complexity of motor drives used in humanoid robots, drones, surgical robotics, and precision-motion systems. 
EPC’s EPC231xx family integrates high- and low-side eGaN FETs, gate drive, level shifting, control interface, and protection functions into a monolithic GaN 100 V ePower™ Stage IC. The accompanying EPC91128–EPC91131 three-phase BLDC/PMSM inverter platforms give engineers a complete environment to evaluate current capability, sensing, protection, thermal performance, and different PWM interfaces. 
The platforms operate across a recommended 14–80 V range (48 V typical) and support switching frequencies from 20 to 150 kHz. Complementary PWM versions maximise control flexibility, while single-PWM-input-pin versions reduce control-line count and wiring complexity—an increasingly important advantage as robotic systems scale to dozens of motors. 
“In multi-axis robotics, power density is only part of the challenge,” said Marco Palma, VP Motor Drive Marketing and System Engineering at EPC. “Integration must also simplify control, protection, sensing, thermal management, and wiring. The EPC231xx family and its evaluation platforms give engineers a validated starting point that can be replicated efficiently across many motor axes.”

HS Hyosung Unit to Invest 1.2 Trillion Won in Ulsan Silicon Anode Plant
Three-Phase Expansion in Ulsan-Mipo Industrial Complex Through 2030 to Reach 20,000 Tons a Year
Joint Venture With Belgium's Umicore Marks Group's First New Business After Spinoff
Society | Published 2026.09.14. 11:29:26 
| By Jang Ji-seung jjs@sedaily.com 
| Summary | Save 
A A A 
Ulsan Mayor Kim Sang-wook and Lee Ki-soo, chief executive of HS Hyosung Energy Solution Korea, sign a memorandum of understanding on investment in a new silicon anode material plant for secondary batteries at Ulsan City Hall on Nov. 14. Photo courtesy of Ulsan City ULSAN — HS Hyosung Energy Solution Korea, a joint venture set up by HS Hyosung Group with Belgium-based Umicore, has chosen Ulsan as its production base for next-generation battery materials. The company will invest a combined 1.2 trillion won ($860 million) through 2030 to build silicon anode production capacity.
The city of Ulsan said on the 14th that it signed a memorandum of understanding on the new silicon anode plant at the mayor's office in city hall, with Ulsan Mayor Kim Sang-wook and HS Hyosung Energy Solution Korea CEO Lee Ki-soo in attendance.
Under the agreement, HS Hyosung Energy Solution Korea will build a large-scale production plant in three phases on a site in the Ulsan-Mipo National Industrial Complex. Silicon anodes offer higher energy density and faster charging than conventional graphite anodes, making them a key material for extending the driving range of electric vehicles and shortening charging times.
The investment will be carried out in stages through 2030. In the first phase, the company will spend 300 billion won to complete its first plant, MPK-1, with annual capacity of 5,000 tons by the first quarter of 2028. In the second phase, it will invest another 300 billion won to add 5,000 tons of annual capacity between the first quarter of 2028 and the third quarter of 2029. In the final phase, it will spend 600 billion won from the first quarter of 2029 to the third quarter of 2030 to add 10,000 tons of annual capacity. Once the third phase is complete, total annual capacity will reach 20,000 tons.
HS Hyosung Energy Solution Korea said it will give priority to hiring Ulsan residents during both construction and operation of the plant to help create local jobs. The city will provide administrative support, including expedited permits and approvals, to keep the project on track.
The investment is the first new business HS Hyosung Group has pursued in earnest since its spinoff. It also carries symbolic weight, establishing an advanced materials base in Ulsan, the group's birthplace and manufacturing hub.
"We selected Ulsan, the birthplace of the Hyosung Group, as our first investment site, and we will become an advanced materials company that grows together with the region," CEO Lee said. "We will help strengthen the competitiveness of global supply chains by developing next-generation battery materials into a national strategic industry."
"This will be a turning point for Ulsan to lead the global supply chain in core next-generation battery materials," Mayor Kim said. "We will spare no administrative support to develop Ulsan into a center of the future secondary battery industry."

Hs Hyosung Energy Solution Korea signs Ulsan deal, accelerates silicon anode push 
Ulsan pact sets 2028 debut for first 5,000-ton silicon anode plant amid 1.2 trillion won investment plan 
입력 2026.09.14. 09:42 
조선비즈 구글 검색 먼저 보기 
HS Hyosung Energy Solution Korea said on the 14th it will sign an investment agreement with Ulsan City to build a new plant to produce silicon anode material. HS Hyosung Energy Solution Korea is a joint venture established by HS Hyosung Group with Umicore to make a full-fledged entry into the silicon anode material business, a core material for next-generation batteries.
HS Hyosung Energy Korea CI. /Courtesy of HS Hyosung 
HS Hyosung Energy Solution Korea plans to prioritize hiring Ulsan residents during the construction and operation of the new plant, contributing to local job creation and revitalizing the regional economy.
Ulsan City plans to work closely with corporations to ensure the investment proceeds without a hitch and takes root stably in the region, and to provide active administrative support, including various permits and approvals.
HS Hyosung Energy Solution Korea plans to invest 1.2 trillion won in the Ulsan–Mipo National Industrial Complex to establish a mass-production system for silicon anode material by 2030. The investment will proceed in three total phases. Under the investment agreement with Ulsan City, the company will first inject 300 billion won to build MPK-1, a silicon anode material plant with an annual capacity of 5,000 tons, by the first quarter of 2028.
Lee Ki-su, CEO of HS Hyosung Energy Solution Korea, said, "Through this investment, we plan to foster the next-generation battery material industry as a national strategic industry and help strengthen the global supply chain competitiveness of key sectors such as semiconductors, shipbuilding, and defense," adding, "In particular, as we have selected Ulsan, the birthplace of Hyosung, as the first investment site, we will establish ourselves as corporations that grow together with the region by reorganizing advanced production bases and creating jobs."
Kim Sang-wook, Ulsan mayor, said, "This agreement will further strengthen Ulsan's competitiveness in core materials for next-generation batteries and serve as an important opportunity to lead the global supply chain of the secondary battery industry," adding, "We will spare no administrative support to foster Ulsan as the hub of the future secondary battery material industry and to ensure it leads to quality jobs in the region and shared growth of related industries."

content_text:
South Korea's Largest Private Offshore Wind Farm Off Sinan to Expand to 900MW by 2031
Add preferred source 
South Korea's largest privately led offshore wind farm, Jeonnam 1, is now operating off the coast of Sinan County in South Jeolla Province. SK Innovation E&S and Denmark's Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners (CIP) formed a joint venture and invested 900 billion won (approximately $670.2 million) to build the 96MW facility. The turbines stand 227 meters tall—comparable to Seoul's 63 Building—and the site's average annual capacity factor is in the low-to-mid 30% range. Developers plan to break ground on Phases 2 and 3 by the end of next year, expanding total capacity to 900MW by 2031. The fourth-quarter fixed-price contract auction is a critical inflection point, while the 15MW turbine supply chain and a levelized cost of energy around 300 won per kWh (approximately $0.22) remain key challenges. The project is expected to serve as a cornerstone power source for the Honam semiconductor cluster's electricity demand.
Key Elements 
Jeonnam Offshore Wind Power SK Innovation E&S CIP Kim Jin-cheol Jeonnam Offshore Wind Phase 1 Honam Semiconductor Cluster Doosan Enerbility Siemens Gamesa Sinan County 
Off the coast of Jaeun-myeon in Sinan County, South Jeolla Province, South Korea's largest privately led offshore wind farm is now in operation. Jeonnam Offshore Wind Phase 1, featuring ten turbines arranged in two rows and standing 227 meters above sea level, has become a new pillar of power supply for South Korea's Honam region since beginning commercial operations late last year.
The facility is operated by Jeonnam Offshore Wind Power, a joint venture established with SK Innovation E&S holding a 51% stake and Danish energy investment firm Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners (CIP) holding 49%. The project required a total investment of 900 billion won (approximately $670.2 million) to install ten turbines rated at 9.6MW each. Total installed capacity is 96MW, generating enough electricity to power roughly 90,000 households for a year.
The scale of each turbine is substantial. When the blades reach their highest point, they extend 227 meters above sea level—nearly matching the 250-meter-tall 63 Building in Seoul. Each blade measures 97 meters in length and weighs 44 tons. The tower anchored to the seabed weighs 600 tons, while the nacelle housing the core components weighs 520 tons—together exceeding 1,000 tons.
The blades are designed to achieve maximum output at wind speeds of 12 meters per second. They rotate nine times per minute and automatically shut down for safety when wind speeds exceed 28 meters per second. At the actual operating site, each blade rotated at a different speed, and some were completely still—a vivid demonstration of the intermittency that remains an inherent limitation of renewable energy.
The site's average annual capacity factor is in the low-to-mid 30% range. However, there is significant variation by time of day, with utilization climbing to the 60% range in the early morning hours and remaining relatively high during winter. This stands in contrast to solar power, which is strongest during daytime and summer. If the two energy sources complement each other, they are expected to help meet the electricity demand of the Honam semiconductor cluster that the South Korean government is promoting.
The government estimates that once the Honam semiconductor cluster reaches full scale, the South Jeolla region will require an additional 6.3GW of power—exceeding the entire Honam region's electricity demand of approximately 5GW last year. Offshore wind is considered well-suited to South Korea's geography, surrounded by sea on three sides, due to its higher generation efficiency compared to onshore wind.
Jeonnam 1 also carries significance for domestic supply chain localization. Approximately 75% of major components and installation equipment were procured through partnerships with South Korean companies, and it is the first domestic offshore wind project to adopt a monopile foundation structure. While cheaper than the conventional jacket method, monopiles are highly sensitive to seabed conditions, which had deterred developers from attempting them. Following Jeonnam 1's success, other developers are now considering adopting monopile foundations.
Developers are now preparing for the next phase. Construction of Phase 2 (399MW) and Phase 3 (399MW) is scheduled to begin by the end of next year, with plans to build out a combined complex approaching 900MW by 2031. Phases 1, 2, and 3 combined would represent roughly nine times the current capacity—equivalent to about 64% of a single large-scale nuclear reactor (based on 1.4GW).
The project's critical inflection point is the fourth-quarter fixed-price contract auction for offshore wind. If selected as a project operator, the site's location—which does not overlap with military training zones or shipping lanes—is expected to allow for expedited permitting. Kim Jin-cheol, Vice President at SK Innovation E&S, said, "The Jeonnam 2 and 3 zones are situated away from the boundaries of military training and vessel traffic areas that require permitting. If selected in the auction, development can proceed faster than in other zones."
The key concern is project cost. SK Innovation E&S estimates that offshore wind development costs have risen to approximately 4.5 trillion won (approximately $3.4 billion) per 500MW of installed capacity. High interest rates have worsened project financing conditions, while rising raw material prices and currency fluctuations have added further pressure.
The turbine supply chain is another variable. Phases 2 and 3 plan to deploy 15MW-class turbines, but no domestically commercialized product currently exists in South Korea. Doosan Enerbility is preparing assembly production in partnership with Siemens Gamesa, but concerns have been raised about potential price competitiveness gaps versus European products. Chinese turbines are approximately 40% cheaper than European ones, but the developers' policy is to exclude them due to security concerns.
The levelized cost of energy (LCOE) is another challenge to address. South Korea's current fixed-bottom offshore wind LCOE stands at approximately 300 won per kWh (approximately $0.22)—considerably more expensive than large-scale nuclear power (50–70 won per kWh). Higher generation costs translate into higher power procurement expenses, which could pressure electricity rates upward.
International examples suggest a breakthrough is not out of reach. In the United Kingdom, offshore wind generation costs fell sharply after cumulative installed capacity surpassed 4GW. South Korea's cumulative installed capacity remains at just 0.35GW. The government has set targets to deploy 4GW annually by 2030 and reach cumulative capacity of over 25GW by 2035, but whether actual installation keeps pace with the plan remains to be seen.
Industry players are hoping for expanded inflows of public capital, including the National Growth Fund. Funding from the National Growth Fund has already been confirmed for the Sinan-Ui offshore wind project in South Jeolla Province. Voices in the industry argue that government support is needed to back early-stage projects until generation costs achieve competitiveness.
Vice President Kim emphasized, "By the time Jeonnam Phases 2 and 3 are completed, we expect to be able to reliably supply electricity to the Honam semiconductor cluster. Once the project reaches a certain scale, generation costs will naturally decline—what we need is the capacity to endure until that point."

content_text:
Is Moderna, Merck's mRNA cancer vaccine win the start of a 'personalized medicine revolution'?
By
Marissa Russo 
Sep 11, 2026 9:00am 
Moderna 
Merck & Co. 
mRNA 
cancer vaccine 
"This is going to catalyze so much incredible ... innovation," Johns Hopkins University's Jeff Coller, Ph.D., told Fierce. (wildpixel/Getty Images)
The announcement from Merck & Co. and Moderna last month that their mRNA cancer vaccine had successfully lengthened patient survival in a phase 3 study affirmed the two companies' years of hard work and reignited hopes for the field of personalized medicine.
There's a lot riding on exactly how well intismeran autogene—alternatively known as V940 or mRNA-4157—performs, and the companies have held back any detailed data for a future medical meeting. But intismeran seems to do its best work against resected late-stage melanoma when paired with the standard-of-care immunotherapy Keytruda. 
Merck and Moderna's INTerpath-001 trial enrolled 1,137 patients who had previously had their cutaneous melanoma surgically removed. These participants either received intismeran along with Keytruda, or Keytruda alone. According to the August update, the group who received the adjuvant therapy showed statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvements in recurrence-free survival, the study's primary endpoint, and survival without a distant metastasis, a secondary endpoint.
Since that announcement, experts and industry insiders have suggested to Fierce that the news has not only renewed hopes in the intismeran program, which hit a regulatory hurdle back in 2024, but also boosted prospects for other biopharmas exploring mRNA as a vehicle for personalized cancer treatments.
What continues to make oncology treatments so difficult to perfect is that every type of cancer is different and even patients who have the same cancer have tumors that behave differently under the same treatments. Being able to customize a vaccine to each patient’s particular tumor would be a boon.
“I think it's the start of a personalized medicine revolution,” said Jeff Coller, Ph.D., a professor of RNA biology and therapeutics at Johns Hopkins University, when speaking with Fierce about the intismeran update. “This is going to catalyze so much incredible research and development and innovation.”
When the full data do become available, investors will be looking to see whether intismeran could be used against other cancers and as broadly as Keytruda, said Myles Minter, Ph.D., a William Blair analyst. 
“We’ll have to see what the data look like, but if they look really good and this is a stepwise change in efficacy, this is standard-of-care shifting,” he told Fierce.
Knock-on effect
By the time the markets closed on the day of the therapy's phase 3 announcement, Moderna’s stock was up 177% —but it wasn't alone. Share prices were up as much as 20% for other biotechs that are playing in the mRNA arena, such as Arcturus Therapeutics. 
The San Diego-based biopharma has been developing therapies for infectious diseases, such as COVID-19 and influenza, as well genetic conditions like cystic fibrosis and ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency, the most common urea cycle disorder. Currently, its COVID-19 vaccine Kostaive is approved in Japan, the U.K and the EU.
Arcturus’ approach to mRNA therapies is to leverage self-amplifying mRNA, which CEO Joseph Payne argued is better at expressing the antigen than personalized antigens. Arcturus’ self-amplifying mRNA includes a replicase, which allows for more and sustained protein production. 
The uniqueness of this type of mRNA also means it can be administered at lower doses with higher antibodies and for a longer time, Payne told Fierce. In combination with this platform, Arcturus has developed a lipid nanoparticle delivery system, Lunar, which it's testing in a phase 2 trial as an inhalable mRNA therapy for patients with cystic fibrosis.
Arcturus entered into a research pact with London-based Achilles Therapeutics in 2024 to explore personalized mRNA cancer vaccines. The goal of the collaboration is to combine Achilles' AI platform Peleus, which identifies patient neoantigens, with Arcturus’ self-amplifying mRNA technology.
For now, Arcturus' broader strategy focuses on infectious and life-threatening genetic diseases, but Payne does think the technology can be applied to cancer. “I think the field is moving towards oncology,” he said.
German biopharma BioNTech is already in that race. Even before its pivot to become a “fully integrated immunotherapy powerhouse,” the company had been working on its FixVac mRNA cancer vaccine platform , which uses a fixed combination of mRNA-encoded non-mutated tumor antigens in an effort to enhance the stability of mRNA in the body. Vaccines from the platform are designed to target antigen-presenting dendritic cells and trigger a strong immune response.
The lead candidate, dubbed BNT113, is an mRNA cancer immunotherapy candidate that encodes a fixed set of two oncoproteins that are frequently found in human papillomavirus type 16 positive (HPV16+) solid tumors. BNT113 has reached phase 2/3 development in head and neck cancer with a readout on the first of its two primary endpoints anticipated this year.
Ugur Sahin, M.D., and Özlem Türeci, M.D., founded BioNTech in 2008 to research mRNA technology, which was overlooked in science at the time. The company made its name during the COVID-19 pandemic, with the release of Pfizer-partnered Comirnaty, the first COVID-19 vaccine to get a full approval from the FDA .
In collaboration with Genentech, BioNTech has another flagship personalized mRNA platform known as individualized neoantigen-specific immunotherapy (iNeST). The iNeST platform encodes up to 20 patient-specific neoantigens and uses a unique delivery platform called a lipoplex that enables administration of the vaccines to key “boot camps of the immune system,” like the spleen, lymph nodes and bone marrow, a BioNTech representative explained to Fierce. 
With this approach, the company aims to eliminate polyclonal residual disease and is focusing on cancers for which immunotherapies have not worked well, such as pancreatic cancer. 
BioNTech recently scrapped a phase 2 study of an iNeST candidate called autogene cevumera in patients with surgically removed stage 2 or 3 colorectal cancer. Genentech originally told Fierce that this move was down to “more deaths in the vaccine arm in this specific patient population,” with a representative from BioNTech later clarifying that the “decision was not safety-related” and was instead due to a “numerical imbalance in overall survival between treatment arms.”
BioNTech noted that a phase 2 trial evaluating autogene cevumera in combination with checkpoint inhibitors and chemotherapy in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma “will not be affected and continues as planned.”
Another contender in the programmable mRNA field is Strand Therapeutics, which is studying two self-replicating mRNA therapies that deliver IL-12, an immune signaling protein, for treatment of solid tumors. STX-001 was designed to be injected directly into tumors and is being tested in phase 1/2 trials as a monotherapy or in combination with Keytruda for triple-negative breast cancer and melanoma. Strand is concerned not just with delivery, cell-selective expression, and durability but also with controlling the RNA after delivery, according to CEO Jacob Becraft, Ph.D.
Jacob Becraft, Ph.D.
(Strand Therapeutics)
“Some of the most powerful therapeutic proteins have been difficult to use safely throughout the body,” Becraft said in an interview with Fierce. “Our goal is to make those proteins usable by programming where and how they are produced.”
Phase 1 data from the study unveiled at the American Society of Clinical Oncology conference last year included a confirmed complete response and multiple partial responses from patients with immune checkpoint inhibitor-refractory solid tumors.
Strand, which has received Big Pharma backing from the likes of Regeneron, Amgen and Eli Lilly, has another key asset in the form of STX-003. The programmable mRNA cancer immunotherapy was developed to be injected intravenously and enable IL-12 expression in tumors, allowing for a possible multi-pronged approach to targeting disease at multiple sites.
“What excites me most is the possibility of opening up an entirely new set of usable medicines,” Becraft said. “Once we can reliably deliver and control RNA in a particular cell type, we can explore multiple therapeutic payloads using that foundation. That could substantially accelerate how quickly new biological insights become treatments.”
Looking back
Moderna and Merck may have captured the headlines with intismeran, but the two companies have been working together since 2016 to develop a series of mRNA vaccines. mRNA, short for messenger ribonucleic acid, makes it possible for every cell in the body to transform DNA code into an active protein the cell uses to do a specialized job. Although scientists first discovered these naturally occurring little helpers in 1961, it would take them three more decades to wrangle mRNA as a tool for vaccination against viruses and yet another three decades before that application found mass commercial success in humans. 
Along this slow rise, squaring up mRNA vaccine technology against the vagaries of cancer specifically has remained elusive. All of this time and anticipation is latched to intismeran's journey to FDA approval and the impact such an approval would have on other mRNA therapies.
“This program sits at the convergence of decades of advances in cancer research, genomic sequencing, computational biology and informatics,” said Michelle Brown, Ph.D., Moderna's oncology lead for intismeran. “mRNA is the technology that was able to galvanize and bring it all together.” 
Moderna has centered itself on mRNA medicines since its founding in 2010, but as with BioNTech, it was the COVID-19 pandemic that pushed the technology mainstream. Moderna developed the Spikevax vaccine as part of Project Warp Speed during President Trump’s first term.
“Those policies that were made by the Trump administration really have led to this new revolution in neoantigen personalized cancer approaches,” Coller told Fierce.
Despite this initial support, the tone changed last year when the Department of Health and Human Services announced a plan to end mRNA vaccine work funded by the Biomedical Advanced Research and Development Authority (BARDA), a major escalation of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s campaign against both vaccines and mRNA in general.
Moderna executives explained to Fierce a few months later that this shift in sentiment had encouraged the biopharma to focus its efforts on cancer rather than infectious disease. Still, the company secured a major success in the latter category last month when the FDA made mFlusiva the first-ever mRNA flu vaccine to receive regulatory approval in the U.S.
Accelerated approval, again 
Intismeran is customizable because it targets neoantigens, proteins that appear on the surface of cancer cells that are specific to each patient, almost like “tumor fingerprints,” Moderna's Brown told Fierce. Before receiving intismeran, each patient had their tumor sequenced and scientists designed the vaccine to fit its unique signature.
Michelle Brown, Ph.D.
(Moderna)
To make this match, the tumor's sequence was funneled into a bioinformatic algorithm that ranked the mutations based on expression, not just presence. The algorithm assessed whether antigens were “up and available for the immune system to see,” Brown said, and which neoantigens would be able to generate the best killer T-cell response while also recruiting other immune cells to the tumor.
For Merck and Moderna, 34 neoantigens was the ideal number, compared with iNest’s 20. Intismeran’s phase 2 study, which launched in 2019, cut the risk of disease recurrence by 49% at five years of follow-up . “It was the first time that we saw an inkling that a doublet could improve upon [Keytruda] standard of care,” Brown said. “It also showcased the ability to create benefit on recurrence-free survival and distant metastasis-free survival.”
The wider intismeran program encompasses a total of nine phase 2 and 3 trials in indications beyond melanoma, such as non-small cell lung cancer and renal cell carcinoma.
But it hasn't all been plain sailing for the vaccine. Back in 2024, intismeran encountered a regulatory setback when the biopharmas attempted to secure an accelerated approval pathway and the FDA rebuffed them. At the time, Moderna said it would not return to seek accelerated approval until it had a “substantially enrolled” phase 3 trial in for an adjuvant melanoma therapy. 
That patience appears to have paid off with the recent announcement of the trial's primary endpoint win. Despite holding back the data, the companies said they plan to engage with regulators on filing approval submissions for a combo regimen of intismeran and Keytruda. Moderna’s Brown remains steadfast in waiting for the full phase 3 data readout, although she is excited about what is to come with intismeran and the wider field of immunotherapy.
“It increases our confidence in the biological rationale and the power of what mRNA can provide, and it definitely showcases the clinical benefit in melanoma,” Brown said. “It gives us learnings for the rest of the portfolio overall.”

content_text:
Hydro all aboard for railcar recycling effort
The global aluminum producer is working with Siemens Mobility to recycle aluminum from end of life railcars.
Hydro calls the Train2Train project a demonstration of its commitment to low-carbon aluminum and circular economy, showing how collaboration across the value chain can keep valuable materials in circulation.
Photo courtesy of Norsk Hydro ASA 
By
Brian Taylor, Senior Editor 
Published September 11, 2026
Listen to article 
/ 
Recycled-content aluminum producer Norsk Hydro ASA says it is working in collaboration with several other companies in Europe to recycle aluminum recovered from decommissioned trains and then produce new rail industry components.
Hydro, which is based in Norway and has aluminum melt shops in Europe and the United States, says it is working alongside rail industry supplier Siemens Mobility, Germany-based metals recycling firm TSR Group and Austria-based steelmaker Voestalpine on the Train2Train project.
In a pilot study that is part of the project, Hydro will melt recycled aluminum from decommissioned trains at its facility in Ghlin, Belgium. 
The aluminum comes from TSR Group, which has dismantled the rail vehicles and separated aluminum from steel with the aim of recycling the metals into new rail parts. Hydro receives the recyclable aluminum, while Voestalpine receives the ferrous scrap.
After being melted, the aluminum scrap will be processed into extrusion billets, which will be used as input material at a Hydro extrusion facility in Harderwijk, Netherlands. 
Hydro calls the Train2Train project a demonstration of its commitment to low-carbon aluminum and the circular economy, showing how collaboration across the value chain can keep valuable materials in circulation.
“Aluminum can be recycled repeatedly without losing its properties,” says Piotr Chmielewski, a vice president with Hydro Extrusions Europe. “By combining recycling expertise, digital traceability and manufacturing capabilities, we can create new opportunities for circular solutions in the rail industry. This project builds on Hydro’s ambition to accelerate the transition towards a more circular and low-carbon aluminum industry.”
Hydro says it supplies a variety of aluminum products for the rail industry, supporting manufacturers with “lightweight, durable and recyclable materials for applications including train structures, interiors and components.”
The Train2Train project aims to demonstrate that the materials from a decommissioned train can be recovered, recycled and reborn into a new one. 
In the United States, Sweden-based steelmaker SSAB has collaborated with metals recycler Alter Trading, St. Louis, and railcar builder Greenbrier Companies, Lake Oswego, Oregon, in a project that establishes a similar loop .
Hydro  says, “At a time when global supply chains are under increasing pressure, gaining greater control over material flows is becoming increasingly important. The project brings together the full value chain, from dismantling and recycling to material processing and manufacturing, with each partner playing a critical role in creating a transparent and circular material loop.”

Amkor Technology increases Arizona semiconductor campus investment to $12bn
By
Alexa Hornbeck 
| Published: 10-Sep-2026 
Design & Build 
Containment 
The semiconductor packaging and test services provider will add 60,000 sqm of cleanroom space to its Arizona campus, taking the site’s total cleanroom footprint to approximately 93,000 sqm
Amkor Technology is expanding its planned investment in a new advanced semiconductor packaging and test campus in Arizona to approximately $12bn, as customer commitments drive the addition of a second phase.
The company said demand has surpassed the 33,000 sqm of cleanroom capacity planned for Phase 1 of the campus.
Phase 2 will add a further 60,000 sqm, bringing the total cleanroom area across the site to around 93,000 sqm. 
The project is being developed as a multi-phase semiconductor manufacturing campus in Peoria, Arizona, with capabilities spanning wafer bump, probe, assembly and test.
Amkor said the expansion will increase the scale of advanced packaging manufacturing in the US, with the combined phases expected to support a workforce of more than 3,500 Arizona-based employees. 
The campus is intended to become the first US outsourced semiconductor assembly and test (OSAT) production site providing advanced packaging at high volume, offering customers a domestic turnkey manufacturing platform.
Construction of Phase 2 is expected to begin in late 2027, with completion targeted for the end of 2029. The wider campus covers approximately 170 acres, allowing for further expansion in response to customer demand. 
Amkor originally broke ground on the Arizona campus in October 2025, when the planned investment stood at $7bn across two phases. The project was initially planned to provide more than 750,000 sq ft of cleanroom space. 
The latest expansion follows a series of developments around Amkor’s US advanced packaging strategy.
In June, the company announced a 10-year agreement with TSMC covering advanced packaging and testing services in Arizona, while in July it announced a multi-year partnership with NVIDIA supported by a $1.5bn advanced packaging and development agreement.
“This next phase reflects the confidence our customers have placed in Amkor, the critical role advanced packaging plays in enabling the future of semiconductor innovation, and the strategic importance of our Arizona campus," said Kevin Engel, President and CEO of Amkor Technology.
The Arizona campus will support semiconductor applications including artificial intelligence, data centres, smartphones, automotive and wearable devices.

content_text:
FDA clears Bayer’s Hyrnuo in first-line lung cancer, amping up Hernexeos rivalry
By
Donavyn Coffey 
Sep 9, 2026 4:33pm 
Bayer 
NSCLC 
tyrosine kinase inhibitor 
FDA approval 
“This approval underscores the potential of precision medicine to transform outcomes by matching the right patients to the right therapy at the right time,” said Christine Roth, executive vice president, global product strategy and commercialization at Bayer. (Bayer)
In an accelerated decision , the FDA expanded Bayer’s Hyrnuo indication, granting first-line approval for a rare tumor type in patients with non-small cell lung cancer. 
Before the expansion, Hyrnuo was available only after other NSCLC treatments failed. But the FDA’s latest go-ahead makes the tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) an initial therapy option for any patient with locally advanced or metastatic non-squamous NSCLC whose tumors test positive for HER2 tyrosine kinase domain activating mutations. 
The expanded indication was won using data from Bayer’s ongoing phase 1/2 Soho-01 trial, in which Hyrnuo demonstrated a 75% objective response rate in previously untreated patients. Six percent of patients showed a complete response, and 70% showed a partial response to the twice-daily oral medication, Bayer said Wednesday. Responses lasted more than six months for 73% of patients.
This subtype of lung cancer patients are often non-smokers and “historically have a poor prognosis,” said Soho-01 lead investigator, Xiuning Le, M.D., Ph.D., of The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center, in a statement. 
“This approval underscores the potential of precision medicine to transform outcomes by matching the right patients to the right therapy at the right time,” added Christine Roth, executive vice president, global product strategy and commercialization at Bayer.
The accelerated approval means Bayer will have to continue to prove Hyrnuo’s clinical benefit through post-marketing confirmatory studies. The latest approval may hinge on the outcome of Bayer's phase 3 trial, Soho-02, which is evaluating Hyrnuo versus standard of care in treatment-naïve patients with advanced HER2-mutant NSCLC. 
Related
'Better every quarter': Bayer CEO stays course on turnaround plan as pharma sales underwhelm in Q2 
The Hyrnuo expansion follows a similar first-line approval for the drug's main competitor , Boehringer Ingelheim’s oral TKI Hernexeos, in February. Because HER2 mutations represent only 2% to 4% of the NSCLC patient population, the battle for market share between the two drugs is expected to be fierce. 
Both Bayer and Boehringer's target the same mutated tumors, although Hyrnuo is specifically designated for locally advanced or metastatic non-squamous NSCLC, while Boehringer’s label holds a small distinction for unresectable or metastatic cancer.
Hyrnuo received initial FDA approval last November , just three months after Hernexeos. In that instance, the FDA signed off on the medicine as a second-line treatment after Hyrnuo logged a 71% objective response rate in the phase 1/2 Soho-01 trial in patients who received prior systemic therapy but not one that specifically targets HER2 mutations.
Earlier this year, Hyrnuo was approved in China as a second-line treatment for unresectable, locally advanced or metastatic HER2-mutant NSCLC. The drug was also granted breakthrough therapy designation in the country to expedite its potential use as a first-line treatment, and it has also secured a first-line nod in Japan.

From Power Lines to Mine Shafts: Lidar Expands the Reach of Drone Mapping
September 9, 2026 by Miriam McNabb Leave a Comment 
Ouster partnerships with GeoCue and Flyability show how next-generation lidar is supporting applications above infrastructure and deep inside confined spaces 
Two recent partnerships from lidar developer Ouster highlight the expanding role of lidar in commercial drone operations. The applications range from surveying utility infrastructure from the air to mapping confined industrial spaces where GPS and conventional cameras may not work.
Ouster and Flyability announced this week that they are building on a five-year technology partnership centered on Flyability’s Elios 3. The collision-tolerant drone is designed for inspection and mapping inside mine shafts, wastewater tunnels, tanks, industrial vessels and other difficult or hazardous spaces.
The announcement follows a partnership unveiled last week between Ouster and GeoCue . GeoCue plans to integrate Ouster’s Rev8 OS1 Max digital lidar into its TrueView drone mapping systems for utility and infrastructure surveying.
 
Together, the two applications illustrate how improvements in lidar range, resolution and data capture could support increasingly diverse drone operations.
Mapping Where GPS and Cameras Fall Short
Flyability’s Elios 3 combines a protected, collision-tolerant airframe with Ouster’s compact OS0 lidar. Lidar data feeds the drone’s SLAM and mapping systems, supporting real-time localization, flight stability and collision avoidance.
Those capabilities become especially important inside structures where GPS is unavailable. Darkness, airborne dust and surfaces without distinctive visual features can also limit camera-based navigation.
The system allows operators to capture measurable 3D representations of assets while conducting inspections, reducing the need for workers to enter potentially hazardous areas.
“Flyability has demonstrated how digital lidar can create real operational value when it is taken into environments that conventional surveying systems cannot easily reach,” said Ouster CEO Angus Pacala. “Our collaboration brings together rugged, high-density 3D sensing and a unique aerial inspection platform, helping industrial teams understand critical assets while reducing the need for people to enter hazardous spaces.”
Flyability is now evaluating Ouster’s newer Rev8 lidar technology for future inspection workflows. Ouster says the Rev8 generation increases range and resolution while adding native color to the 3D data.
“Our collaboration with Ouster began with a shared ambition: to capture reliable 3D data in places where people should not have to go,” said Adrien Briod, CTO at Flyability. “Ouster’s lidar has become a critical part of the Elios 3 mapping platform. Bringing our teams together at INTERGEO gives us the opportunity to show surveying professionals how aerial access and high-performance lidar are already changing the way complex industrial environments are documented and understood.”
The companies will demonstrate the technology at INTERGEO 2026, taking place September 15-17 in Munich, Germany.
Taking the Same Technology to Large-Scale Mapping
The GeoCue partnership puts the latest Ouster technology into a very different operating environment.
GeoCue is expanding its TrueView product line with options using Ouster’s 256-channel Rev8 OS1 Max lidar. The companies are targeting utility and infrastructure applications, including power line mapping and long-corridor surveys.
Ouster says the sensor can detect targets with 10% reflectivity at distances up to 200 meters. A smaller spot size and tighter beam are designed to help resolve thin features such as power lines and structural edges. The system also provides native color lidar data, combining color and 3D information at the sensor level.
GeoCue selected the sensor after joint flight testing and firmware tuning in Huntsville, Alabama.
“We are moving America’s drone surveying onto American sensing by pairing our TrueView payloads with Ouster’s Rev8 OS1 Max,” said Frank Darmayan, CEO of GeoCue. “This transition allows us to offer our customers a compliant, high-performance solution that delivers the survey-grade data they depend on for critical infrastructure monitoring and large-scale mapping projects.”
The Rev8 OS1 Max is also compliant with Build America, Buy America Act requirements, an important consideration for some federally funded infrastructure projects.
Lidar Expands Across Drone Applications
The two partnerships demonstrate very different uses of the same underlying sensing technology.
With GeoCue, lidar is designed to capture precise data across large infrastructure assets from above. With Flyability, lidar helps a drone navigate and map spaces that may be inaccessible from outside and unsafe for people to enter.
In both cases, the value extends beyond creating a point cloud. Lidar increasingly supports navigation, localization and autonomous operation while also generating the 3D data required for inspection and mapping.
As sensors gain range, resolution and richer data, that overlap between perception and data collection could become increasingly important. The drone is no longer simply carrying a mapping sensor. In applications such as the Elios 3, the sensor that creates the map can also help the aircraft understand where it is and operate where other navigation technologies fall short.
