title: Moderna's Cancer Vaccine Nears Commercialization…South Korean Oncologist Flags 'Real-World Hurdles' - BigGo Finance
query: ("Moderna" OR "Moderna Inc") (Korea OR Korean) after:2026-09-01 before:2026-10-01
content_text:
Moderna's Cancer Vaccine Nears Commercialization…South Korean Oncologist Flags 'Real-World Hurdles'
Add preferred source 
Moderna and Merck's jointly developed personalized mRNA cancer vaccine has succeeded in a Phase 3 melanoma trial, opening a new chapter in cancer treatment. Dr. Dae Ho Lee, a professor at Asan Medical Center in Seoul, explained that unlike conventional cancer drugs, this therapy analyzes each patient's tumor to design a bespoke treatment. However, significant real-world barriers remain: custom manufacturing takes three to six weeks, and the cost and infrastructure burden are substantial. AI plays a pivotal role in antigen selection, an area that constitutes each company's proprietary trade secrets. Melanoma commercialization is projected for 2027, but South Korea faces hurdles including the absence of manufacturing and logistics systems and health insurance reimbursement issues. Phase 3 results for lung cancer are expected as early as next year.
Key Elements 
Moderna Merck Dae Ho Lee Asan Medical Center mRNA cancer vaccine Keytruda Intismeran Autogene Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer melanoma 
As the personalized messenger RNA (mRNA) cancer vaccine posts positive Phase 3 results in melanoma and is hailed as opening a new era in cancer treatment, clinical practitioners are pointing to cost, infrastructure, and time as the next set of real-world challenges—separate from the technology's promise.
Dr. Dae Ho Lee, a professor of medical oncology at Asan Medical Center in Seoul, is participating in the lung cancer clinical trial of "Intismeran Autogene," the personalized mRNA cancer vaccine co-developed by Moderna and Merck. In an interview with Hankyung Business, he explained that this therapeutic strategy starts from a fundamentally different premise than conventional cancer drugs.
Existing targeted therapies and immunotherapies work by selecting from a menu of already-manufactured drugs to find one that suits the patient. An mRNA cancer vaccine, by contrast, compares the patient's tumor tissue with normal tissue to identify neoantigens that appear only on cancer cells, then designs a treatment exclusively for that patient. Dr. Lee likened the difference to "off-the-rack clothing versus a bespoke suit."
The potential has been confirmed, but the mountain ahead is formidable. Custom manufacturing requires the entire pipeline for each patient: tumor analysis, antigen selection, mRNA design, manufacturing, and transport. The process currently takes roughly three to six weeks—a substantial wait for stage 4 patients who need treatment urgently.
"Having the technology alone isn't enough," he stressed. "Connecting the entire chain—from analysis to manufacturing to logistics—costs money." In practice, the most viable approach is to begin standard treatment first while the personalized vaccine is being manufactured, then administer it as an add-on once ready.
Antigen Selection Is the Make-or-Break…AI Holds the Key
The most challenging part is identifying the "truly good antigens." Cancer cells generate millions of protein data points, and it is nearly impossible to determine in advance which antigens will actually deliver therapeutic efficacy. Even when computational analysis narrows the field to roughly 100 candidates, there is no way to know how many are genuine winners.
Artificial intelligence is the core enabler of this massive analytical undertaking. Normal and tumor tissue must be precisely compared, and researchers must verify from multiple angles whether the relevant RNA actually expresses well as protein. "Which antigens are ultimately selected and baked into the vaccine is the crux—and that depends entirely on each biotech company's AI algorithms and analytical know-how," Dr. Lee said. This is a company's core trade secret and remains undisclosed.
Commercialization Outlook and South Korea's Reality
On the prospect that melanoma commercialization could begin in 2027, Dr. Lee responded, "I think it's possible." Approvals are likely to come first in the United States, Europe, and China—countries that participated in the clinical trials.
However, regulatory approval and actual clinical use are separate matters. Personalized therapy is not something that can simply be imported and used like a conventional pharmaceutical. A patient's tumor must be sent for analysis, a treatment tailored to that patient must be manufactured, and then it must be shipped back and administered. This requires a dedicated system linking manufacturing and logistics.
"South Korea currently lacks such a system," Dr. Lee pointed out. If treatment costs are prohibitively high and patient volumes are low, companies have little incentive to build separate manufacturing and logistics infrastructure in South Korea. Integration with South Korea's national health insurance reimbursement framework is another critical variable.
Lessons from mRNA Technology and the Challenge for South Korean Biotech
He diagnosed that South Korea's biotech industry has developed around generics over the past 15 to 20 years, leaving innovation underfunded. COVID-19, in particular, was a crucial opportunity to develop mRNA technology firsthand, yet South Korea ultimately failed to produce its own COVID-19 mRNA vaccine.
Cancer mRNA vaccines are far more complex than COVID-19 vaccines. A COVID-19 vaccine targets a single antigen, whereas cancer differs from patient to patient and requires identifying multiple antigens. "Being able to make mRNA doesn't mean you can develop the entire platform," Dr. Lee said. "We need to identify which parts of the overall platform we can be competitive in." He emphasized that just as South Korea has found competitive niches in semiconductors and data centers rather than building AI from scratch, the biotech sector also requires focus and strategic prioritization.
Lung Cancer Trial Results Expected Next Year
For the ongoing Phase 3 non-small cell lung cancer trial involving approximately 900 patients worldwide, Asan Medical Center has already completed enrollment of South Korean patients. Results from this study are expected as early as next year. Separately, another lung cancer trial including stage 4 patients is also underway.
Dr. Lee's outlook is that the next decade will be less about which therapy to use alone and more about finding the optimal combinations of multiple treatments. The combination of CAR-T—which "manufactures soldiers"—mRNA vaccines—which "identify attack targets"—and Keytruda (pembrolizumab)—which "strengthens the soldiers"—could emerge as a key research priority.
On the melanoma trial success, he said, "The significance is that it confirms the personalized mRNA cancer vaccine strategy itself is viable," while adding, "This study is a beginning, not an end." The results confirmed in melanoma must now be validated in other cancer types including lung cancer, and separately in early-stage patients versus advanced and stage 4 patients.

Building on an established relationship spanning multiple years, Wipro will continue delivering end-to-end AI-enabled Digital Workplace Services for ABB's global operations while further enhancing employee experience through advanced automation, AI-powered service capabilities, and workplace modernization initiatives. 
Powered by Wipro Intelligence™ , the unified suite of AI platforms, solutions and transformative offerings, this engagement will modernize ABB’s digital workplace with AI-led, experience-centric capabilities delivered through Wipro’s AI Live Workspace™ and Digital Workplace Services offerings and operationalized through WINGS, Wipro’s AI-powered delivery platform for operations. Through SmartOps, Wipro’s AIOps capability, the focus will be on more autonomous and predictive workplace services, including GenAI-powered self-service, virtual agents, auto-remediation and AI-assisted dispatch. By harnessing telemetry and usage insights, Wipro will optimize device lifecycle management and strengthen endpoint security operations, while supporting ABB’s digital transformation and sustainability ambitions. 
“As ABB operates at global scale with a highly diverse workforce, the reliability, security, and user experience of our digital workplace are critical,” said Ana Jauregui, Head of Consumer Experience, ABB. “Wipro’s ability to deliver standardized services while remaining responsive to local needs will help us drive higher productivity, improve employee satisfaction, and support our long term digital and sustainability ambitions.” 
Madhavan R, Managing Director & Country Head of Switzerland, Wipro Limited , said, “ABB and Wipro share a relationship that has grown over many years, anchored in trust, collaboration, and a common ambition to drive meaningful business outcomes. ABB’s continued confidence in Wipro reflects the strength of this enduring partnership and our shared commitment to innovation. As AI becomes a defining force in the future of work, we are bringing together our expertise and AI-led Digital Workplace capabilities to help ABB create a more intelligent, automated, resilient, and employee-centric workplace experience for colleagues across the globe.” 
This expanded engagement further reinforces Wipro's long-standing presence in the industrial and manufacturing sector, where enterprises are increasingly modernizing workplace operations to improve agility, productivity, and employee experience at a global scale.

Sumitomo Chemical and Gutenberg Co., Ltd. Develop LCP Filament for 3D Printers
Accelerating the Development of High Value-Added Applications in Semiconductors, Communications, Next-Generation Mobility, and Other Fields 
Sep. 1, 2026
Sumitomo Chemical and Gutenberg Co., Ltd. (“Gutenberg”), which is leading the development of high-speed 3D printers produced in Japan, have jointly developed a liquid crystal polymer (LCP) filament and molding technology for 3D printers that use the FFF method (*1) . The Company will accelerate the development of applications in next-generation fields, including functional components that contribute to advances in semiconductors and physical AI.
3D-printed parts 
Robot hand housing 
In recent years, materials capable of handling complex geometries, achieving weight reductions, and integrating parts have been receiving increased interest across advanced industrial fields. For this reason, design and manufacturing using 3D printers have attracted increasing attention. Amid this trend, there is a demand for not only freedom of design, but also for high functionality in resin materials themselves. LCP is a super engineering plastic that combines heat resistance, high strength, low dielectric constant and low dissipation factor, and excellent dimensional stability. As a material for 3D printers, however, its use has been limited due to difficulties in filament formation and molding.
To address these challenges, Sumitomo Chemical has developed a material design and filament formation technology for LCP suited to additive manufacturing. The Company also collaborated with Gutenberg, which develops, manufactures, and sells industrial 3D printers, to examine the molding process and establish a technology that enables stable molding while controlling the unique molecular orientation of LCP. This technology achieves high thermal conductivity and strength comparable to that of aluminum alloys (*2) , while also maintaining lightweight properties. This makes it possible to create complex shapes that are difficult to achieve with injection molding, while also meeting the needs of low-volume, high-mix production.
Going forward, Sumitomo Chemical will expand its efforts into a wide range of fields, including peripheral components for semiconductor manufacturing, humanoid robot-related components that are expected to be put into practical use as physical AI advances, the communications field, and next-generation mobility fields such as eVTOL (*3) . In addition, the Company will accelerate the development of new applications by advancing evaluations of its filament and molded products in collaboration with customers. The Company plans to begin providing samples of this filament in 2026, and it is also looking ahead to future expansion into the space and defense fields.
Sumitomo Chemical will continue to promote the provision of innovative materials and solutions that support next-generation manufacturing. In doing so, the Company will contribute to the creation of new value and the development of society and industry.
(*1) A 3D printing method in which thermoplastic resin is melted, extruded from a nozzle, and stacked layer by layer. 
(*2) The Company evaluated the fracture strength of LCP and aluminum alloy under certain conditions using a test method compliant with standards set by the International Organization for Standardization. 
(*3) Electric Vertical Take-Off and Landing aircraft, commonly referred to as flying cars.

title: Applied Materials Touts 3D Scaling Technologies, Develops New Materials for HBM and CPO - THE ELEC, Korea Electronics Industry Media
source: Google News: THE ELEC, Korea Electronics Industry Media
publisher: THE ELEC, Korea Electronics Industry Media
query: "Applied Materials" (Korea OR Korean) after:2026-09-01 before:2026-10-01
content_text:
Mukund Srinivasan, global group vice president of Packaging and Integrated Materials Solutions at Applied Materials. (Photo: THE ELEC) 
Applied Materials has completed preparations for four key technologies needed for next-generation three-dimensional (3D) semiconductor scaling. The company is also accelerating workforce and infrastructure expansion in line with recent capacity increases by its Korean customers.
Mukund Srinivasan, global group vice president of Packaging and Integrated Materials Solutions at Applied Materials, said at a media briefing at Oakwood Premier Coex Center on Aug. 31 that artificial intelligence (AI) models are becoming increasingly compute-intensive, with their power consumption rising exponentially. "The solution to the industry's key challenge of minimizing power consumption per bit of data is 3D scaling," he said.
The proliferation of AI is exacerbating the "memory wall," a bottleneck between computing and memory. Overcoming it requires more efficient data transmission that moves information quickly while consuming less power. Applied Materials said logic chips, memory and packaging are all rapidly transitioning to 3D structures.
The company also outlined four key challenges in implementing 3D structures and the technologies it has developed to address them. "The most important innovations for 3D scaling are, first, new materials development; second, actual process innovation; then angstrom-level (Å, 0.1 nanometers) process control of processes and equipment; and optimization at each process step," Srinivasan said. "Applied has considerable confidence in its core unit processes and materials, and we are confident that we can also solve the challenges of integrating them."
◇ New Materials for HBM and CPO 
Kim Ji-hye, executive director at Applied Materials Korea, moderates the media briefing. (Photo: THE ELEC) 
New materials development is aimed at easing interconnect bottlenecks inside and outside chips. Resistance and capacitance need to be reduced to increase signal transmission speeds and lower power losses. Applied Materials is seeking solutions through advanced thin-film and plating technologies and new materials research and development (R&D).
The Producer Avila 2 plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition (PECVD) system is one such solution. It can deposit oxide and nitride thin films at low temperatures on the backside of high-bandwidth memory (HBM). Core dies, or DRAM chips, used in HBM are about one-25th the thickness of conventional DRAM dies, making them susceptible to warpage. Applied Materials' solutions also include the Nokota VMax 2 electrochemical deposition (ECD) system for copper plating of ultra-fine through-silicon vias (TSVs) measuring 3 micrometers or less.
More recently, the company has been jointly researching new optical waveguide materials with customers for co-packaged optics (CPO). CPO is a next-generation technology that integrates optical and high-performance electronic chips in a single package. Applied Materials is also developing highly thermally conductive insulating materials that maximize heat dissipation while maintaining electrical insulation to address HBM thermal issues.
◇ 3D Structure and Hybrid Bonding Technologies in Place 
HBM and CPO models. (Photo: THE ELEC) 
The second area, process innovation, requires technologies capable of forming complex 3D structures. Applied Materials has developed and commercialized selective processes that can treat specific areas within 3D structures, as well as bonding technologies that reduce the spacing between chips to near zero.
In particular, the Centura Prime Epi selective epitaxy system for DRAM peripheral circuitry selectively grows silicon germanium (SiGe) and phosphorus-doped silicon (Si:P) in transistor electrode regions, or sources and drains. The technology enables next-generation semiconductor manufacturing by introducing impurities into silicon and precisely controlling their concentration to tune the electrical properties of semiconductors.
Applied Materials also offers Kinex, an integrated die-to-wafer (D2W) hybrid bonding cluster system. D2W bonding directly joins copper and dielectric materials between chips, maximizing input/output (I/O) density and reducing signal delays compared with microbumps. Kinex integrates plasma activation, cleaning, D2W bonding and metrology into a single system, cutting queue time from 13 hours to one hour.
"Applied has a complete portfolio of products for both D2W and wafer-to-wafer (W2W)," Srinivasan said. "We are helping customers more easily determine which combinations and approaches they want to adopt."
Third, as logic and memory processes become more advanced, equipment capable of real-time control and measurement of errors at the nanometer and angstrom scales has become essential. Applied Materials has prepared the Opta Quad chemical mechanical planarization (CMP) system, the VeritySEM 7AP e-beam critical-dimension metrology system and the SEMVision G7AP e-beam defect analysis system. Opta Quad CMP can be used for hybrid bonding and TSVs, VeritySEM 7AP for HBM and chiplet substrates, and SEMVision G7AP for silicon, organic and glass substrates.
◇ EPIC Center and ACCK Link Up as Korea Hiring Continues 
Park Kwang-sun, president of Applied Materials Korea. (Photo: THE ELEC) 
The final area, optimization at each process step, involves integrating interactions among semiconductor manufacturing processes beyond the individual equipment level. Applied Materials is preparing for this through its EPIC (Equipment and Process Innovation and Commercialization) Center and Applied Collaboration Center Korea (ACCK).
Applied Materials' EPIC Center is a $5 billion R&D facility. Companies including Samsung Electronics, SK hynix and Micron are participating. The facility is under construction and is scheduled to open in Silicon Valley in October. It will allow semiconductor companies to jointly coordinate the entire process from early-stage materials development to device design, deposition, planarization and bonding, and validate technologies for mass production. The goal is to significantly shorten the time needed to commercialize new technologies.
ACCK is a next-generation semiconductor R&D collaboration hub being established in Osan, Gyeonggi Province. It will receive foundational technologies and innovative materials developed at the EPIC Center in Silicon Valley and jointly develop them with Korean customers through technology validation. "Once ACCK in Korea is completed, we will connect foundational research and materials innovations developed at the EPIC Center with Korean customers through ACCK in Osan," said Park Kwang-sun, president of Applied Materials Korea. "We will strengthen the support system so new technologies can be directly linked to our customers' mass-production lines in Korea and maximize the pace of innovation."
"We are also making various efforts to ensure there are no gaps in workforce and technical support as our customers expand globally," Park added. "We are having in-depth discussions about workforce expansion not only internally but also with universities and customers, so we do not expect major difficulties."
